vignette:
Minh’s hands, which have always been his greatest asset, now feel like they belong to a stranger. He holds them up in the quiet of my office, turning them over as if examining a foreign object. These are the hands of a carpenter—calloused, strong, capable of shaping raw timber into something beautiful and precise. For most of his 31 years, they have been steady. Now, a fine tremor often runs through them, a vibration that has no business being there. It’s worst in the mornings and when he hears a siren.

Before the incident eight months ago, Minh’s life had a rhythm he understood. He and his wife, Lien, were saving for a down payment on a house. His small business, specializing in custom cabinetry and furniture, was finally gaining a reputation for quality. He loved the smell of cedar in his workshop, the satisfying hum of the table saw, the quiet focus required to join two pieces of wood so perfectly they seemed to have grown that way. He felt a deep sense of pride in creating things that were solid, functional, and meant to last.

The rhythm broke on a Tuesday night in February. He was driving home from a client’s house, later than usual, his mind on the blueprints for a new project. The flashing red and blue lights appeared in his rearview mirror with jarring suddenness. He pulled over immediately, his heart thumping with the mundane annoyance of a traffic stop. He knew he had a broken taillight he’d been meaning to fix.

The officer’s approach was aggressive from the start. Minh, trying to be polite, reached for his registration in the glove compartment. The officer yelled at him to keep his hands on the wheel. The commands were fast, overlapping, and laced with an anger Minh couldn’t comprehend. Confused and startled, he fumbled, his movements becoming clumsy under the glare of the flashlight. That hesitation was all it took. His door was wrenched open and he was pulled from the truck. The next few minutes were a blur of rough hands, the cold shock of pavement against his cheek, and a knee pressing hard into his back, grinding his face into the asphalt. He remembers the smell of gasoline and dirt, the metallic click of handcuffs, and the utter powerlessness of the moment. He was cited for the broken taillight and for “resisting,” then left on the curb, shaking and humiliated, as the patrol car drove away.

He told Lien he had tripped and fallen getting out of the truck. The bruises on his face and ribs faded within a couple of weeks, but a different kind of injury had set in. Sleep became a battleground. He’d jolt awake, heart racing, the feeling of pressure on his back so real he’d gasp for air. He stopped driving after dark, adding hours to his commute by taking convoluted routes on side streets to avoid the stretch of road where it happened.

At work, his focus shattered. The loud whine of the circular saw now makes him flinch. He mismeasures cuts, wasting expensive hardwood. The tremor in his hands makes fine detail work, his specialty, nearly impossible. He feels a constant, simmering anger just below the surface, and it often spills out at Lien over small things, like the placement of a coffee cup. He sees the hurt and confusion in her eyes and hates himself for it. He feels a profound sense of shame—not just for the incident itself, but for his inability to “get over it.” The man who could build a flawless bookcase from scratch now feels fundamentally broken. The blueprints for his own life, once so clear and precise in his mind, are now smudged and unreadable.
